title: What causes the northern lights?

explain.say: Auroras, the northern and southern lights, are curtains of coloured light dancing in the night sky near the poles. They start at the Sun, which constantly blows out a stream of charged particles called the solar wind.

explain.say: Earth's magnetic field acts like a shield, steering most of these particles around the planet. But near the magnetic poles, the field lines dip down and guide some particles into the upper atmosphere.

explain.say: The atoms quickly release that energy as light, a bit like a neon sign. Oxygen glows green and, higher up, red, while nitrogen adds blue and purple. Big solar storms push auroras much further from the poles.

faq.a: A constant stream of electrically charged particles, mostly electrons and protons, flowing out from the Sun at hundreds of kilometres per second.
asks: What comes from the Sun to make auroras?

faq.q: Why are auroras near the poles?
faq.a: Earth's magnetic field lines curve down into the planet near the magnetic poles, guiding charged particles from the Sun into the atmosphere there, in rings around each pole.
asks: Why can't I see the northern lights everywhere?

faq.a: The most common colour comes from oxygen about 100 to 250 kilometres up, which glows green when energised. Oxygen higher up glows red, and nitrogen gives blue and purple.
asks: What makes the colours of the northern lights?

faq.a: The aurora australis is the same glow around the south magnetic pole, seen from Antarctica, southern New Zealand, Tasmania and the far south of South America.
asks: Is there an aurora in the south?

faq.q: When is the best time to see an aurora?
faq.a: On dark, clear nights, close to the Arctic or Antarctic circles and far from city lights. Auroras are brighter and more frequent around the peak of the Sun's 11-year activity cycle.
asks: Where can I see the northern lights?

facts: The Sun's activity rises and falls in a cycle of about 11 years, and auroras are most frequent near its peak.
In May 2024 a strong solar storm made auroras visible unusually far from the poles, as far south as Mexico.

quiz.say: What makes the green light of most auroras?
quiz.show: The green glow of an aurora comes from…

options.show: Oxygen atoms high in the air
options.say: Oxygen atoms high in the air

quiz.why: Particles from the Sun energise oxygen atoms about 100 to 250 kilometres up, and they give off green light.

wrong.1: Auroras glow by themselves, high above the clouds, not by reflection.
wrong.2: Auroras are far above the clouds, and lightning is a different, much shorter flash.
